title: Design and Enforce AI Authorization and Access Controls
intro: Authorisation for AI systems that can act: least privilege and separation of duties across models, pipelines and agents; role, attribute and purpose-based authorisation enforced outside the model, with just-in-time access in place of standing privilege; execution boundaries and API scope limits that set an agent’s real reach; and preventing excessive agency, over-delegation and lateral movement by autonomous agents.
objectives: Apply least privilege and separation of duties to models, tools, pipelines, agents and administrators, and identify toxic combinations
Combine RBAC, ABAC and PBAC through policy decision and enforcement points, and replace standing privilege with just-in-time access
Set execution boundaries and API scopes that limit what agents and code interpreters can run and reach
Prevent excessive agency, over-delegation and lateral movement through minimal tools, attenuation, approvals, segmentation and monitoring

sections.title: Least privilege and separation of duties for AI

scenes.title: Just enough, and never alone
scenes.sub: Least privilege and separation of duties for AI
scenes.say: Two of security’s oldest principles matter even more when software can decide and act on its own: least privilege, and separation of duties. | This video applies both across AI models, pipelines and agentic workflows.

scenes.title: Least privilege, component by component

items.d: No direct access; only via tools

scenes.say: Least privilege means every component gets only the access its job needs. | A model should have no direct access to data or systems; it reaches them only through controlled tools. | Agents get the tools and scopes for their current task, and start read-only. | Tools should offer narrow functions rather than generic ones. | Pipelines use separate credentials for each stage. | Data access is limited by row, column and approved purpose. | And people, including administrators, have no standing access to production models or weights, only elevation when needed.

scenes.title: Generic tools and narrow tools
scenes.say: Tool design is where least privilege is won or lost. | Compare a generic tool that runs any database query with a narrow one that looks up a single order’s status. | If a manipulated agent misuses the generic tool, it could read or delete anything the database credentials allow. The narrow tool limits the damage to one order. | The generic tool has an endless number of cases to test; the narrow one has a small, testable surface. | And policy for a narrow tool is easy to express, while policy for arbitrary queries is very hard. So build narrow tools, and keep generic ones away from agents.

scenes.title: Separation of duties in AI systems

items.d: Agents can’t change their own rights or rules

scenes.say: Separation of duties means no single person, or system, can complete a sensitive process alone. | The people who build a model don’t approve it for production. | Training and deployment use different identities and credentials. | Agents act as makers, not checkers: an agent can propose a payment, but a different party approves it. | Agents can never change their own permissions, prompts or guardrails. | And the most sensitive operations, such as exporting weights or using signing keys, need two people.

scenes.title: Separation of duties across the model lifecycle
scenes.say: Here is separation of duties across a model’s lifecycle. A data steward approves which data may be used, and for what purpose. | Machine learning engineers build and train the model, but can’t approve it. | An independent validator tests and challenges it. | A risk owner approves it for production, in line with its risk tier. | The platform team deploys only approved versions, using credentials the builders don’t hold. | And security operations monitors it in production, independently of the team that runs it.

items: Models reach systems only through narrow, controlled tools
Agents: per-task, read-only first; people: no standing admin
Builders don’t approve; agents propose but don’t approve
No self-modification; two people for crown-jewel operations
scenes.say: To recap. | Models should reach systems only through narrow, controlled tools. | Agents get per-task permissions, read-only first, and people get no standing administrative access. | Builders don’t approve their own models, and agents can propose but never approve high-impact actions. | And no agent may change its own permissions, while crown-jewel operations need two people.

blocks.md:
### Least privilege for AI components
| Component | Least-privilege practice |
|---|---|
| **Model** | No direct credentials or network access; reaches data and systems only through tools that enforce policy |
| **Agent** | A distinct identity (Module 4.5); only the tools and scopes for the current task; read-only by default; write and delete rights only where needed, ideally with approval |
| **Tools and MCP servers** | Narrow, purpose-built functions (*refund up to £200 to the original payment method*) rather than generic ones (*run SQL*, *call any URL*, *execute shell*) |
| **Retrieval** | Document permissions enforced at query time, filtered to what the requesting user may see (Module 1.2) |
| **Pipelines** | Per-stage, short-lived credentials; training can’t deploy, and deployment can’t read raw training data (Module 3.5) |
| **Data** | Row-, column- and purpose-level controls (Module 3.4) |
| **People** | Zero standing privilege for production models, weights and data; just-in-time elevation (Section 2) |

### Separation of duties
Separation of duties (NIST SP 800-53 AC-5; ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A 5.3, segregation of duties) prevents one identity from completing a sensitive process alone. In AI systems, look for **toxic combinations**:
- The same identity can **change training data and approve** the resulting model.
- An agent can **create a payee and pay it**, or **raise and approve** its own purchase order.
- An agent or pipeline can **modify its own permissions, prompts or guardrails**.
- One administrator can **export model weights** without a second approval.
- The team that runs a model is the **only** team monitoring it.

**Maker–checker for agents:** let agents prepare actions (draft the email, stage the payment, propose the change) and route approval to a human or an independent system. A second model reviewing the first is weaker than it looks, because both can be influenced by the same injected content; use deterministic policy checks and human approval for high-impact steps.

### Implementing the principles
- Build an **SoD matrix** of duties that must not be combined, and check role and permission assignments against it, including for non-human identities.
- Use **separate identities** for building, approving, deploying and operating.
- Make **guardrail, prompt and permission changes** go through change control, never through the agent itself.
- **Review** effective permissions regularly, because agents and tools gather rights over time (Module 4.7).

blocks.title: Spot the toxic combination
pairs: An agent can add a new supplier and also pay invoices to it
Maker and checker in one identity
The data scientist who trained a model also signs it off for production
Builder approves own work
An agent can edit the policy file that limits its own tools
Self-modification
One administrator can export model weights with no second approval
Missing two-person control
The only alerts on a model come from the team that runs it
No independent monitoring

blocks.title: PoLP and SoD questions
blocks.md: Prefer **narrow tools**, **per-task scopes** and **read-only defaults** over broad access "for flexibility". If one identity, human or agent, can both **initiate and approve** a sensitive action, the best answer splits those duties.

q.q: A sales assistant agent is given a tool that runs any SQL query against the CRM database, so that it can answer a wide range of questions. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Keep the generic tool, but add a system prompt telling the agent to use only SELECT statements
Replace it with narrow tools for specific lookups, running with read-only, scoped credentials
Give the agent a separate copy of the CRM database, so that queries can’t affect production
Log every query the agent runs, and review the logs at the end of each month for problems
q.why: Narrow, read-only tools limit what a manipulated agent can do and are easy to test and govern. Prompt instructions can be overridden, a copy still exposes all the data, and monthly log reviews only find problems later.

sections.title: Authorisation models and just-in-time access for AI

scenes.title: Deciding what’s allowed, right now
scenes.sub: RBAC, ABAC, PBAC and just-in-time access
scenes.say: Authentication proves who is asking. Authorisation decides what they may do: this request, on this data, for this purpose, right now. | This video applies role, attribute and purpose-based authorisation to AI systems, and shows how just-in-time access removes standing privilege.

scenes.title: Policy decision and enforcement
scenes.say: Modern authorisation separates deciding from enforcing. A request arrives, for example an agent asking a tool for customer records. It carries who is asking, for whom, what action, why, and in what context. | An enforcement point, such as an AI gateway or the tool itself, intercepts it. | It asks a policy engine, which evaluates roles, attributes, the declared purpose and risk signals against policy written as code. | The decision can be allow, deny, or allow with conditions, such as masking some fields or requiring human approval. | The enforcement point applies that decision exactly. | And the decision and its reason are logged, so every access can be explained later.

scenes.title: Three models, one agent
scenes.say: Module 3.4 introduced these models. Here is how they apply to one support agent. | Role-based control asks what role is calling. Attribute-based control asks whether attributes of the caller, resource, action and context match. Purpose-based control asks whether the declared purpose is approved for this data. | So, under role-based rules, support agents may read tickets. Attribute rules narrow that to this customer’s tickets, during this session. Purpose rules allow it only to resolve this case, not, say, to train a model. | Roles give coarse baselines, attributes add fine contextual rules, and purposes enforce data protection and consent. Real systems combine all three.

scenes.title: Just-in-time elevation
scenes.say: Just-in-time access replaces standing privilege with temporary, approved elevation. An engineer requests access, stating the reason and how long they need it. | Low-risk requests can be approved automatically by policy; high-risk ones go to a person. | Access is granted temporarily, scoped to the task, for hours rather than months. | The privileged session is recorded. | Access is revoked automatically when it expires, with no one needing to remember. | And use is reviewed, so misuse or unusual patterns are caught.

scenes.title: Where AI platforms need just-in-time access
scenes.say: On AI platforms, just-in-time access fits six situations. | Write access to the model registry, which controls what reaches production. | Stores of personal or regulated training data. | Exports of model weights, with a second approver. | Changes to an agent’s permissions, such as adding tools or widening scopes. | Break-glass access during incidents: fast, but logged and reviewed. | And agents themselves, which should receive task-scoped tokens that expire when the task ends.

items: Separate decision (policy engine) from enforcement (gateway, tool)
Combine RBAC baselines, ABAC context and PBAC purpose
Decisions can carry conditions: mask, approve, limit
Just-in-time: requested, approved, scoped, recorded, auto-revoked
scenes.say: To recap. | Separate the policy decision from its enforcement in gateways and tools, with policy written as code. | Combine role baselines, attribute context and purpose checks. | Let decisions carry conditions, such as masking fields or requiring approval. | And replace standing privilege with just-in-time access that is requested, approved, scoped, recorded and revoked automatically.

blocks.md:
### Authorisation architecture
- **Policy decision point (PDP):** evaluates requests against policy. Policy-as-code engines such as Open Policy Agent (Rego) and Cedar keep rules versioned, testable and reviewable.
- **Policy enforcement point (PEP):** sits in the request path (AI gateway, tool server, retrieval layer, data store) and applies the decision.
- **Policy information point (PIP):** supplies attributes: user and agent identity, data classification, purpose registry, risk scores.
- **Policy administration point (PAP):** where policies are written, reviewed and approved.

Decisions can include **obligations**: mask fields, redact documents, cap amounts, or require step-up or human approval. Authorisation should be **continuous**: re-evaluated as context changes during a session, not just at sign-in.

### Choosing and combining models for AI
| Situation | Typical approach |
|---|---|
| Which tools an agent type may use | RBAC baseline per agent role |
| Which records an agent may read for a user | ABAC (user, tenant, region, session) plus delegation (Module 4.5) |
| Whether data may be used for a task, such as training | PBAC against registered purposes (Module 3.4) |
| Which documents a RAG system may retrieve | Document-level permissions (ACLs or relationship-based rules) filtered at query time for the requesting user |
| Whether a specific high-value action may proceed | Transaction-level policy (amount, payee, risk) with approval obligations |

### Just-in-time access
- **Zero standing privilege:** administrators hold no permanent production rights; they elevate for a task.
- **Request, approve, grant, record, revoke:** with reasons, time limits and automatic expiry.
- **Risk-based approval:** automatic for low-risk elevation, human approval (and step-up authentication) for high-risk.
- **Break-glass accounts:** for emergencies when normal approval isn’t possible; tightly controlled, monitored, and reviewed after every use (Module 5.5).
- **For non-human identities:** issue short-lived, task-scoped tokens on demand rather than permanent service-account rights.
- **Privileged access management (PAM)** tools typically provide the workflow, credential vaulting and session recording.

blocks.title: Rolling out just-in-time access on an AI platform
items: Find standing privilege
List every human and non-human identity with permanent rights to production models, weights, registries, training data and agent configurations. Include service accounts and shared admin accounts.
Define eligible roles and approvers
Decide who may request each elevation, who approves it, and which low-risk elevations policy can approve automatically.
Set limits
Choose maximum durations, require a reason and a ticket, and add step-up authentication for high-risk roles such as weight export or registry approval (Module 4.5).
Automate grant, recording and revocation
Use a PAM or cloud JIT service so access is granted, session-recorded and removed without manual steps.
Remove what remains, and review
Delete the old standing rights, keep tightly controlled break-glass accounts, and review elevation patterns monthly for misuse and for roles that need redesign.

blocks.title: Authorisation vocabulary
cards: The engine that evaluates a request against policy and returns allow, deny or conditions.
The component in the request path that applies the decision, such as a gateway or tool.
A condition attached to an allow decision, such as masking fields or requiring approval.
No permanent administrative rights; access is granted just in time for a task.
Emergency access outside normal approval, tightly monitored and reviewed after use.

blocks.title: Authorisation questions
blocks.md: Look for **policy enforced outside the model**, in gateways, tools and retrieval, with **context** (attributes, purpose) and **time limits**. Standing administrator access to production AI assets is a red flag; **just-in-time** elevation with approval and recording is usually the best answer.

q.q: Six ML engineers hold permanent administrator rights to the production model registry, though each needs them only a few times a year. What is the BEST change?
o: Keep the permanent rights, but require the engineers to complete annual security training
Remove standing rights, and grant time-limited, approved and recorded elevation when needed
Reduce the number of engineers with permanent rights from six people to three
Share one administrator account between the engineers, so all registry activity is in one place
q.why: Just-in-time elevation removes standing privilege, so a compromised account has no production rights most of the time, and every use is approved and recorded. Training and fewer admins help less, and a shared account destroys accountability.

sections.title: Execution boundaries and API scope limitations

scenes.title: Drawing the edges
scenes.sub: Execution boundaries and API scope limitations
scenes.say: An agent’s real power isn’t what its prompt says. It is what its code can execute, and what its credentials can reach. | This video covers execution boundaries and API scope limitations: the walls and fences that contain what AI components can do.

scenes.title: Boundaries around an agent

layers.label: Resource limits
layers.sub: CPU, memory, time and cost caps

scenes.say: Execution boundaries work in layers. | A tool allow-list: only registered, reviewed tools exist for the agent at all. | Argument constraints: schemas, value limits and allowed targets for every call. | Sandboxed execution for any code the agent writes or runs: isolated, ephemeral, and with no secrets inside. | Network egress control, so the agent and its sandbox can reach only allow-listed destinations. | Data boundaries by tenant, row and purpose. | And resource limits on CPU, memory, time and cost, so a runaway task can’t consume everything.

scenes.title: Broad and scoped tokens
scenes.say: The scope of a token sets the blast radius of a mistake. | A broad token can read, write and delete everything. A scoped token allows specific actions only. | A broad token covers every mailbox and file. A scoped token covers, say, one mailbox and one folder. | A broad token lasts for months. A scoped token lasts only as long as the task. | So if a broad token is misused by a manipulated agent, the result can be an organisation-wide breach. With a scoped token, the impact is small and contained.

scenes.title: Designing scopes for agents
scenes.say: Design scopes along six dimensions. | By action: separate read, write and delete rights. | By resource: a specific tenant, folder or record, not everything. | By amount: caps on payment values, record counts and message volumes. | By time: tokens that expire when the task ends. | By audience: tokens valid for one API only. | And deny by default, so anything not explicitly granted is refused.

items: Real power = what code can run and credentials can reach
Allow-list tools; constrain arguments; sandbox code
Control egress, data boundaries and resource use
Scope tokens by action, resource, amount, time and audience
scenes.say: To recap. | An agent’s real power is what its code can run and its credentials can reach, not what its prompt says. | Allow-list tools, constrain their arguments, and sandbox any code execution. | Control network egress, data boundaries and resource use. | And scope every token by action, resource, amount, time and audience, denying everything else.

blocks.md:
### Execution boundaries
| Boundary | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Tool allow-list** | Agents see only registered, reviewed tools; MCP servers approved through an internal registry (Module 4.1) |
| **Argument constraints** | JSON schemas; allowed values and ranges; payee and domain allow-lists; maximum record counts |
| **Sandboxed code execution** | Code interpreters in containers or microVMs with no secrets, no access to internal networks, read-only base images and teardown after each task (Module 4.2) |
| **Browser and computer-use agents** | Isolated browser profiles, domain allow-lists, no saved passwords or payment details, human confirmation for purchases and submissions |
| **Network egress** | Deny by default; allow-listed destinations; proxies that log and inspect outbound calls |
| **File system** | Access only to a task workspace, never to home directories, credentials or system files |
| **Data and tenancy** | Per-tenant indexes or namespaces in vector databases; row-level security; purpose checks |
| **Resources** | Quotas on CPU, GPU, memory, run time, tokens and spend (Module 3.6) |
| **Cloud guardrails** | Permission boundaries and organisation-level policies that cap what any role, including agent roles, can ever be granted |

### API scope limitations
- **OAuth scopes:** request the narrowest scopes; prefer separate read and write scopes; avoid catch-all scopes such as full mailbox or full drive access.
- **Audience restriction:** resource indicators (RFC 8707) bind a token to one API, so it can’t be replayed elsewhere.
- **Fine-grained, transaction-level authorisation:** Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396) let a token describe a specific action, such as one payment of a stated amount to a stated payee, which suits agents acting on single tasks.
- **Server-side limits:** the API, not the agent, enforces value caps, rate limits and allowed operations.
- **Consent screens:** show users exactly what an agent will be allowed to do, in plain language.

### Common boundary failures
- A code-interpreter sandbox that can reach the cloud metadata service or internal APIs.
- A "read-only" agent whose token also includes write scopes because they were bundled.
- A browser agent logged in to an administrator’s session.
- A tool that accepts any URL, allowing server-side request forgery into internal systems.

blocks.title: The helpful code interpreter
blocks.md: A data analysis assistant writes and runs Python in a container to answer questions about uploaded spreadsheets. During a test, a spreadsheet contains hidden instructions, and the generated code reads environment variables and sends them to an external address. The container holds the assistant’s cloud credentials and has unrestricted internet access.

q.q: Which change MOST directly removes the impact of this attack?
o: Add instructions to the system prompt telling the assistant never to read environment variables
Run the code in an ephemeral sandbox with no credentials and no outbound network access
Scan every uploaded spreadsheet with antivirus software before the assistant opens it
Limit the assistant to answering questions about spreadsheets smaller than one megabyte
q.why: With no secrets inside and no egress, injected code has nothing to steal and nowhere to send it. Prompt instructions can be overridden, antivirus doesn’t detect natural-language instructions, and file size has nothing to do with the attack.

blocks.title: Boundary questions
blocks.md: When an agent or code interpreter is tricked, ask **what it could reach**. The best answers shrink that reach: **sandbox without secrets**, **deny-by-default egress**, **narrow scopes** and **server-side limits**, rather than relying on the model to refuse.

q.q: An email assistant needs to draft replies for a user to review. Its OAuth token currently grants full read, send and delete access to every mailbox in the organisation. What is the BEST scope?
o: Keep full access, because broad scopes avoid errors when the assistant needs something new
Read access and draft creation for that user’s mailbox only, with sending left to the user
Full access to the user’s own mailbox, including the rights to send and delete messages
Read-only access to every mailbox, so it can find related conversations across the company
q.why: The task needs reading and drafting in one mailbox, so the token should allow exactly that, with the human sending. Other scopes add send, delete or organisation-wide reach the task doesn’t need.

sections.title: Preventing excessive agency, over-delegation and lateral movement

scenes.title: When agents go too far
scenes.sub: Excessive agency, over-delegation and lateral movement
scenes.say: Most agent incidents aren’t caused by clever attacks on the model. They happen because an agent had more power than its task needed, passed that power on, or used it to reach systems it should never have touched. | This video covers how to prevent excessive agency, over-delegation and lateral movement.

scenes.title: Three ways agents overreach
rows: More tools, rights or autonomy than needed
Passing on more authority than a task needs
Using one foothold to reach other systems
A mailbox tool that can also delete
A sub-agent handed the user’s full token
scenes.say: Agents overreach in three related ways. | Excessive agency means having more tools, permissions or autonomy than the task needs. Over-delegation means passing on more authority than a task needs. Lateral movement means using one foothold to reach other systems. | For example: a mailbox tool that can delete as well as read; a sub-agent handed the user’s full token; or an agent’s credentials reused to reach unrelated systems. | And the main controls are, respectively: least privilege with approvals; down-scoped, task-specific tokens; and segmentation with a separate identity for every agent.

scenes.title: Attenuate authority at every hop
scenes.say: In a chain of agents, authority should shrink at every hop. This is called attenuation. The user has full rights on their own account. | The orchestrator receives authority only for this trip. | A research agent gets read-only web search, and nothing else. | A booking agent gets the right to make one booking, up to five hundred pounds, and only after the user approves it. | And an external partner’s agent receives only the itinerary details it needs, never the user’s profile or payment credentials. If any agent in the chain is manipulated, the damage is limited to its own small slice of authority.

scenes.title: Layered defences against excessive agency
scenes.say: OWASP lists excessive agency as a top risk for language model applications, and defences work in layers. | Giving agents only the tools and functions they need means an unneeded delete tool simply doesn’t exist. | Least-privilege permissions mean an over-broad credential is never issued. | Human approval for high-impact actions stops an unapproved payment, even if the agent has been manipulated. | And monitoring with rate limits catches runaway bulk actions before they spread.

scenes.title: Stopping lateral movement
scenes.say: Six controls stop agents being used as stepping stones. | Give every agent its own identity and credentials, so compromising one doesn’t unlock the others. | Segment networks and allow-list destinations, so each agent reaches only its own tools. | Never forward tokens: credentials are bound to one audience and never passed along. | Guard shared memory and context, because poisoned content written by one agent can steer others. | Watch for new paths: unfamiliar tools, hosts or call sequences. | And contain fast: revoke a single agent’s identity without stopping every other agent.

items: Excessive agency: more tools, rights or autonomy than needed
Over-delegation: attenuate authority at every hop
Lateral movement: per-agent identity, segmentation, no forwarding
Layer minimal tools, least privilege, approvals and monitoring
scenes.say: To recap. | Excessive agency means more tools, rights or autonomy than the task needs. | Prevent over-delegation by attenuating authority at every hop in a chain of agents. | Prevent lateral movement with per-agent identities, segmentation, and no token forwarding. | And layer minimal tools, least privilege, human approval and monitoring.

blocks.md:
### Excessive agency (OWASP LLM06:2025)
OWASP identifies three root causes:
- **Excessive functionality:** tools that do more than needed, such as a document tool that can also delete, or an "open-ended" tool that runs shell commands or arbitrary URLs.
- **Excessive permissions:** tools that run with credentials broader than the task, such as a reporting tool with write access to the database.
- **Excessive autonomy:** high-impact actions taken without independent verification or approval.

Mitigations include minimising tools and the functions inside them, avoiding open-ended tools, running actions in the **user’s context** with their permissions (delegation, Module 4.5), requiring **approval** for high-impact actions, **complete mediation** (authorisation checked in downstream systems, not just in the agent), and monitoring with rate limits.

### Over-delegation
- **Attenuation:** each delegation narrows scope, audience, amount and lifetime; never widen authority down a chain.
- **Delegation depth limits:** cap how many hops a task can pass through, and record every hop (token exchange actor chains, Module 4.5).
- **Capability-style tokens:** some token formats let the holder add restrictions before passing a token on, but never remove them, which makes attenuation enforceable.
- **External agents:** share only the data and authority a partner’s agent needs; verify its identity and treat its outputs as untrusted (Module 4.1).
- **Consent:** users should see and approve what is delegated on their behalf.

### Lateral movement by agents
Agents are attractive pivots: they hold credentials, reach many systems and can be steered by content. Controls:
- **Per-agent identities** and credentials, never shared service accounts (Module 4.5).
- **Network segmentation** and deny-by-default egress (Section 3; Module 4.2).
- **No token passthrough or forwarding**; audience-bound tokens only (Module 4.1).
- **Shared memory and vector stores** treated as attack paths: write controls, provenance and validation of stored content.
- **Detection:** unusual tool sequences, new destinations, privilege use spikes and agent-to-agent calls outside known patterns (Module 5.3).
- **Containment:** per-agent kill switches and revocation (Module 5.5).

### Zero trust for agents
Apply zero trust principles (Module 4.1): never assume an agent is trustworthy because it is internal; authenticate and authorise every call; give minimal, time-bound access; and assume compromise, so limit and watch what each agent can reach.

blocks.title: Name the overreach
pairs: A summarisation agent’s tool can also delete documents
Excessive functionality
A reporting agent connects with a database administrator account
Excessive permissions
An agent sends external emails with no review step
Excessive autonomy
An orchestrator gives a sub-agent the user’s full access token
Over-delegation
A compromised agent’s credentials are used to reach the HR system
Lateral movement

blocks.title: Excessive agency questions
blocks.md: When an agent does damage, ask three questions: **did it need that tool**, **did it need those permissions**, and **should that action have needed approval**? The best answers remove the unneeded capability, scope the credentials, and add approval or limits, rather than retraining or re-prompting the model.

q.q: An orchestrator agent passes the user’s full OAuth token to every sub-agent it calls, including a third-party summarisation agent. What is the BEST fix?
o: Encrypt the token before passing it, so sub-agents can use it without reading it
Exchange it for down-scoped, short-lived tokens for each sub-agent’s specific task
Ask the third-party provider to confirm in writing that it won’t misuse the token
Pass the token only to sub-agents running inside the organisation’s own network
q.why: Attenuated, task-specific tokens limit each sub-agent to what it needs, and an external agent should get the minimum of all. Encryption doesn’t reduce authority, written assurances aren’t controls, and internal agents can be compromised too.

quiz.q: Why are narrow, purpose-built tools safer for agents than generic ones?
o: They run faster, because they make fewer calls to the database server
They limit what a manipulated agent can do, and are easier to test and govern
They don’t need any authentication, because their functions are so limited
They let the agent write its own queries when the narrow function isn’t enough
quiz.why: A narrow tool caps the impact of misuse and has a small, testable surface that policy can describe precisely.

quiz.q: Which situation is a separation of duties failure in an AI system?
o: Two teams run separate models for different products in the same cloud account
An agent can both create a new supplier and approve payments to that supplier
A model is monitored by the security operations centre as well as its own team
Training and deployment pipelines use different service identities and keys
quiz.why: Creating a payee and paying it are maker and checker duties, which shouldn’t sit with one identity.

quiz.q: Why is a second model a weak checker for a first model’s proposed actions?
o: Second models always cost more than human reviewers at scale
Both can be influenced by the same injected content, so errors may pass together
Regulators prohibit any one AI model from checking another AI model’s proposed output
Second models can’t read the output that the first model produces
quiz.why: Model-based checks share the same weaknesses as the model they check. Deterministic policy and human approval are stronger for high-impact steps.

quiz.q: What is the role of a policy enforcement point in AI authorisation?
o: To write and approve new access policies for the organisation each year
To sit in the request path and apply the policy engine’s decision
To train the model to refuse requests that break the access policy
To store the passwords that users need for each AI application
quiz.why: Enforcement points, such as gateways, tools and retrieval layers, intercept requests and apply allow, deny or conditional decisions.

quiz.q: Which access model checks whether a request’s declared purpose is approved for the data?
o: Role-based access control, using each user’s job title
Purpose-based access control, against approved purposes
Discretionary access control, set by each data owner
Mandatory access control, based on clearance labels
quiz.why: PBAC ties access to registered, approved purposes, which directly enforces purpose limitation and consent.

o: The need to authenticate administrators when they sign in
Standing privilege that sits unused for most of the time
The need to log what administrators do during sessions
All approval steps for high-risk administrative tasks
quiz.why: Elevation is granted for a task and revoked automatically, so compromised accounts hold no production rights most of the time.

quiz.q: What defines an agent’s real power?
o: The wording of its system prompt and the instructions in it
What its code can execute and what its credentials can reach
The size of the model it uses and its benchmark scores
The number of users who are allowed to talk to it each day
quiz.why: Prompts can be overridden. Execution boundaries and credential scopes set the actual limits on what an agent can do.

quiz.q: Which sandbox setting MOST reduces the risk of a code interpreter leaking secrets?
o: A larger memory allowance, so that code doesn’t crash during analysis
No credentials inside, and no outbound network access by default
A faster CPU, so that tasks finish before an attacker can act
Running the sandbox in the same network as the production database
quiz.why: With no secrets present and deny-by-default egress, injected code has nothing to steal and nowhere to send it.

quiz.q: What do resource indicators and token audiences achieve?
o: They make tokens last longer, so that agents re-authenticate less often
They bind a token to one API, so it can’t be replayed elsewhere
They let one token work for every API in the organisation
They hide the token’s contents from the API that receives it
quiz.why: Audience restriction stops a token issued for one service from being accepted by another, preventing replay and confused deputy attacks.

quiz.q: Which is an example of excessive autonomy?
o: An agent that summarises internal documents using a read-only enterprise search tool
An agent that sends emails to customers with no review or approval step
An agent that can call only three tools, each with narrow scopes
An agent whose actions are logged and monitored in real time
quiz.why: Excessive autonomy means high-impact actions happen without independent verification or approval.

quiz.q: What does attenuation mean in a chain of agents?
o: Each agent adds its own permissions to the token it passes on
Authority narrows at every hop: scope, amount, audience and lifetime
Agents pass the user’s full token along so that no step fails
The final agent in the chain decides which permissions to keep
quiz.why: Attenuation ensures each delegated agent holds only the slice of authority its task needs, limiting damage if one is manipulated.

quiz.q: Why should shared agent memory be treated as an attack path?
o: Shared memory uses too much storage for large deployments
Poisoned content written by one agent can steer the others that read it
Shared memory makes agents slower to respond to their users
Regulators require each agent to have a completely separate memory store of its own
quiz.why: Content stored by a compromised or manipulated agent can spread instructions to others, so writes need controls, provenance and validation.

exam.q: An HR assistant agent can read employee records, update salary fields, and approve salary changes it has proposed. Which change BEST applies separation of duties?
o: Keep the current design, but log every salary change the agent makes for later review
Let the agent propose salary changes, with approval by an authorised manager in a separate step
Remove the agent’s ability to read employee records, so it can’t see any salary information
Ask the agent in its system prompt to double-check every salary change before approving it
exam.why: Splitting proposal (maker) from approval (checker) means no single identity, and especially no manipulable agent, completes a sensitive change alone. Logging detects but doesn’t prevent, removing reads breaks the use case, and prompts aren’t controls.

exam.q: A data science team’s shared service account can modify training datasets, run training, and mark models as approved in the registry. What is the BEST first remediation?
o: Rotate the service account’s credentials every month and keep the same permissions
Split the duties across separate identities, and remove registry approval from the build team
Enable detailed logging on the account, and review the logs whenever an incident occurs
Restrict the account so that it can be used only from the office network during work hours
exam.why: The account combines data change, build and approval: a toxic combination that lets one compromise poison and promote a model. Separate identities with approval held by independent roles fix the root cause. Rotation, logging and location limits don’t.

exam.q: A RAG assistant answers staff questions from a document store. Junior staff report seeing excerpts from board papers they can’t open directly. Where should the fix be applied?
o: In the system prompt, instructing the model never to quote from any confidential board documents
In the retrieval layer, filtering results to the documents the requesting user may access
In the user interface, hiding answers that mention the word “board”
In the training data, removing board papers from the model’s pre-training corpus
exam.why: Authorisation must be enforced where content is selected: retrieval should only return documents the user is entitled to see. Prompts and keyword filters are bypassable, and RAG content isn’t in the model’s training data.

exam.q: During an incident at 2 a.m., an engineer needs immediate access to a production model’s serving cluster, but the usual approver is unreachable. What should the access design provide?
o: A permanent administrator account for each on-call engineer, used only in emergencies
Controlled break-glass access: fast, time-limited, fully logged and reviewed afterwards
The approver’s password, kept in a sealed envelope in the operations room for emergencies
No access until the approver is available, whatever the impact of the incident
exam.why: Break-glass access balances speed with control: it works without normal approval, but is limited, monitored and reviewed. Standing admin accounts and shared passwords destroy least privilege and accountability, and refusing access can worsen the incident.

exam.q: A browser automation agent books meetings for executives. During testing, it navigates to an attacker’s page that instructs it to visit the company’s internal admin portal, where it is already signed in. Which boundary MOST directly prevents harm?
o: A system prompt telling the agent to ignore instructions it finds on web pages
An isolated browser profile with no internal sessions, and a domain allow-list for the task
A faster model that finishes each booking before any attacker has a chance to interfere with the agent
Asking executives to check the agent’s browser history at the end of each day
exam.why: An isolated profile without privileged sessions, plus allow-listed domains, removes both the reachable target and the path to it. Prompt instructions can be overridden, speed is irrelevant, and history checks only detect afterwards.

exam.q: A procurement agent can raise purchase orders of any value with any supplier, and does so automatically when a request seems valid. A manipulated request leads to a £48,000 order with a fraudulent supplier. Which combination BEST prevents a recurrence?
o: Retraining the agent on thousands of examples of fraudulent purchase requests and invoices
Supplier allow-lists, value caps, and human approval above a set threshold
A disclaimer in the agent’s replies saying that orders may contain errors
Moving the agent to a larger model that is harder to manipulate
exam.why: Removing excessive permissions (any supplier, any value) and excessive autonomy (no approval) stops a manipulated agent completing a high-impact action. Retraining, disclaimers and bigger models still rely on the model resisting manipulation.

exam.q: A security review finds that twelve internal agents share one service account, which can reach the CRM, finance and HR systems. Any one agent being manipulated could reach all three. What should be done?
o: Keep the shared account, but monitor it far more closely for any unusual activity across all three systems
Give each agent its own identity with access only to its systems, and segment the networks
Rename the service account so attackers are less likely to recognise it
Allow the shared account to be used only during business hours
exam.why: Per-agent identities with minimal access and network segmentation stop one compromised agent becoming a path into every system. Monitoring alone, renaming and time windows leave the shared reach in place.
